title: 36 Hours in Ocean City, Md.
abstract: OCEAN City, the 130-year-old honkytonk town ''down the ocean,'' is undergoing a transformation. The 10-mile-long peninsula between the Atlantic and Isle of Wight and Assawoman Bays, an infamous destination for hormonal teenagers and beloved by blue-collar families as an inexpensive seashore getaway, is going upscale. There are still more tattoo parlors, miniature golf courses and dive bars than you can count, and Route 1 (aka Coastal Highway and Philadelphia Avenue) is still used as a drag strip by muscle cars and road-rocket motorcycles. But merchants are also starting to cater to an influx of high-end condominium buyers who want flavored martinis and $100 tasting menus. Nevertheless, Ocean City's main attraction remains the endless diversions that appeal to all -- sport fishing, parasailing, arcades, skateboard parks and miles of wide, sandy public beaches.  ALICIA AULT    Friday    5 p.m.  1 -- Sitting at Ducks on the Bay    Been trapped in the traffic that brings nearly 300,000 people to Ocean City on a summer day? Exit off the Route 50 bridge and drop in on the end-of-day scene at M.R. Ducks (311 Talbot Street on the Bay, 800-659-7703), above, a favorite of charter captains and crews. The name is a play on Maryland Eastern Shore dialect, in which ''them are'' is pronounced as ''em ahr.'' Sidle up to the gazebo bar and follow the local lead by ordering a can of domestic beer ($2.50). There's live music on the weekends. One recent night, a guitarist held court by using a beer bottle, a baseball cap and a woman's behind as his slide. The cheese-encrusted crab dip in a French bread bowl ($9) will take the edge off your hunger.    7:30 p.m.  2 -- Sunset Overture    They start packing in early at Fager's Island (201 60th Street on the Bay, 410-524-5500) to score prime sunset-viewing spots on the west-facing deck or a cozy perch among the palms on the beach. Order a South of the Border ($9), made with Patrón Silver tequila and Cointreau and served in a blue-salt-rimmed martini glass, to toast the day's end. The 1812 Overture plays, ending just as the sun dips under the horizon, eliciting a burst of applause.    9 p.m.  3 -- Dinner in the First State    All that glass-lifting will create an appetite. Just over the Delaware line on Fenwick Island is Nantucket's (Route 1 at Atlantic Avenue, 302-539-2607), a white-tablecloth restaurant oozing New England charm. Start with the scallops américaine ($14), three jumbo sea scallops with toppings that vary nightly, including grape tomatoes and lump crabmeat set off by black pepper and cumin. As an entree, the lobster shepherd's pie ($36), two five-ounce lobster tails layered over sautéed wild mushrooms and wilted spinach and perched on a mountain of garlic mashed potatoes, scores for creativity. Go for the brownie dessert; it's a quagmire of chocolate chips, vanilla ice cream, whipped cream, chocolate sauce and caramel.    11 p.m.  4 -- Tip On In     Slide back to Maryland via Liquid Assets (9301 Coastal Highway, 410-524-7037). The liquor store's garish plate-glass front belies the magic within: a handsome dark wood bar, surrounded by rattan chairs and tables, and a loungelike seating area with Oriental rugs and silk-upholstered sofas. Patrons can order their passion from the top-shelf bar or select from the 1,600 wines on the shelves ($10 corkage fee). Plenty of cigars in the humidor.    Saturday    10:30 a.m.  5 -- Going Coastal    After breakfast, head two miles north of Ocean City to get wet at Coastal Kayaks (Route 1 on Assawoman Bay, Fenwick Island, Del.; 302-539-7999), where kayaks rent for $15 an hour. Coastal also offers lessons and guided tours. There are plenty of water scooters and boats on the bay, but it's easy to elude them. A half-hour paddle gets you across the bay and up a marshy salt creek that soon becomes too narrow and shallow for anything but a great blue heron to pass.    1 p.m.  6 -- The Requisite Crab Feast    What's Ocean City without crabs? Avoid the all-you-can-eat purveyors who either fudge on their crustaceans' provenance (Maryland and Virginia tend to have limited harvests) or charge excessively for miniature specimens. With its tropical décor and reggae soundtrack, Bahama Mama's (221 Wicomico Street on the Bay, 410-289-0291) looks dangerously like a tourist trap, but it's the real deal. Dozens run $29 to $69, depending on size, and they arrive piping hot, coated in spicy seasoning and demanding to be washed down with a cold beer or a frosty margarita.    3 p.m.  7 -- Strolling the Boards    Join the multitudes on Ocean City's famous -- and clean -- boardwalk, which starts at the inlet and continues for three miles to 27th Street. Drop the children at Trimper's Amusements (South First Street on the Boardwalk, 410-289-8617), which has been owned by the Trimper family for more than a century. Or stroll on, taking in the T-shirt shops, arcades and airbrush-and-henna tattoo offerings. At North Second Street, gawk at the Ocean Gallery (410-289-5300), whose exterior -- plastered with hand-painted slogans on wood scavenged from old buildings -- ranks as a fine piece of outsider art.    8 p.m.  8 -- Seafood Anthem    Drive off the beaten tourist path to the Marlin Moon Grille (12806 Ocean Gateway, 410-213-1618), an up-and-comer in the 1960's-vintage Francis Scott Key Motel in West Ocean City. Run confidently and convivially by Gary Beach, the restaurant pays homage to sport fishing. A crispy quesadilla stuffed with huge lumps of crab, shrimp, artichoke hearts and creamy melted pepper jack cheese ($11) gets taste buds tingling. A seasonal combination platter ($29) -- a sautéed soft-shell crab, three jumbo grilled shrimp and a heavenly crab cake, all piled onto Yukon Gold potatoes smashed with roasted corn, along with an assortment of local vegetables -- will make you swoon.    10 p.m.  9 -- Rock 'n' Reggae    Get irie at Seacrets (49th Street on the Bay, 410-524-4900), which bills itself as ''Jamaica, USA.'' The owner, Leighton Moore, opened a small Caribbean-flavored bar in 1988, which has since morphed into a warren of tiki shacks holding 18 bars, two stages -- one features a rock band nightly, the other a reggae band -- and a maximum of 3,300 guests, many of them dancing. A dress code after 6 p.m., barring baggy shorts and sleeveless undershirts, among other items, is strictly enforced. Weekend cover charges start at $5 at 5 p.m. and top out at $10 at 10 p.m. Seacrets, above, is also a daytime happening: flop on a float and eat lunch, drink and watch the frolicking hot bods.    Sunday    10 a.m.  10 -- Hitting for the Cycle    Maybe a little cycling is in order to counterbalance all that eating and drinking. St. Martin's Neck Road, below, in the Isle of Wight Wildlife Management Area is perfect: a flat stretch of asphalt that meanders through a saltwater marsh, then past chicken houses, farm plots and cornfields. Bring a backpack to carry the fresh zucchini, corn, tomatoes and cantaloupes you'll want to buy from the locals' wagons. You can have them with the take-out brunch you pick up at Rippon's Seafood (120th Street Bayside, 410-524-5500).    THE BASICS  Visiting Ocean City       Ocean City is a three-hour drive from the Baltimore and Washington airports. US Airways Express flies from Philadelphia and Washington to the Salisbury-Ocean City-Wicomico Regional Airport, 30 miles from town. Motorists from New Jersey and points north can use the Cape May-Lewes Ferry (800-643-3779, www.capemaylewesferry.com).      There are some 10,000 hotel rooms representing almost every major chain.     The 23 one-bedroom suites at the Lighthouse Club at Fager's Island (56th Street on the Bay, 410-524-5400) are $180 to $295, lower after Oct. 9.      The recently renovated Inn on the Ocean (1001 Atlantic Avenue, 410-289-8894) overlooks the lively boardwalk but is calm inside. Fall rates for its six rooms range from $180 to $260.
